clinicalPearls: Presents with the sudden painless onset of floaters, cobwebs, a reddish haze, or, with dense bleeding, profound loss of vision
Proliferative diabetic retinopathy and retinal tears (with or without detachment) are among the commonest causes, alongside retinal vein occlusion and trauma
A key priority is to identify a retinal tear or detachment, as these are urgently treatable causes
When the fundus cannot be seen because of dense blood, B-scan ultrasound is essential to look for a retinal tear or detachment
The loss of the red reflex and inability to visualise retinal detail on ophthalmoscopy indicate significant haemorrhage
Initial management often involves upright rest to allow blood to settle inferiorly and improve the view, with treatment of the underlying cause once identified
Persistent non-clearing haemorrhage or an associated retinal detachment is managed surgically with vitrectomy
In children, non-accidental injury must be considered, and spontaneous haemorrhage warrants a search for an underlying vascular or neovascular cause
reference.pathophysiology: Vitreous haemorrhage is extravasation of blood into or around the vitreous cavity. It occurs when abnormal new vessels (as in proliferative diabetic retinopathy or ischaemic vein occlusion) bleed, when normal retinal vessels are torn during posterior vitreous detachment or a retinal tear, or when trauma ruptures vessels. Blood disperses through the vitreous gel, scattering light and obscuring vision. Clearance is slow because the avascular vitreous reabsorbs blood inefficiently, and long-standing blood can lead to fibrosis and tractional complications.
additionalDifferentials: Retinal tear or rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
Age-related macular degeneration with subretinal bleed, or other neovascular disease
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundus examination of both eyes when the view allows
B-scan ultrasonography when the retina cannot be visualised, to exclude a tear or detachment
Assessment of the fellow eye for clues to the underlying cause (e.g. diabetic changes)
Optical coherence tomography and fluorescein angiography once the media clear
Systemic evaluation for diabetes, hypertension, and bleeding tendency as appropriate
redFlags: An underlying retinal tear or detachment requiring urgent treatment to preserve vision
Sudden profound visual loss with an obscured fundus needing prompt ultrasound assessment
Neovascularisation from proliferative diabetic retinopathy or ischaemic vein occlusion requiring timely treatment
Vitreous haemorrhage in a child raising concern for non-accidental injury
Bilateral haemorrhage or associated neurological symptoms suggesting Terson syndrome
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the cause; haemorrhage from a posterior vitreous detachment often clears well, whereas bleeding from proliferative retinopathy or an associated retinal detachment carries a higher risk of recurrence and permanent visual loss without treatment.
pitfalls: Failing to perform B-scan ultrasound and missing an underlying retinal detachment behind dense blood
Attributing the bleed to an obvious cause without examining for a retinal tear
Overlooking non-accidental injury in a child with vitreous haemorrhage
Delaying treatment of proliferative retinopathy while awaiting spontaneous clearance
management: Upright rest with head elevation to let blood settle inferiorly and clear the visual axis
Urgently identify and treat any retinal tear or detachment, using laser retinopexy or cryotherapy for tears and surgical repair for detachment
Treat the underlying cause, with panretinal photocoagulation and intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy for proliferative retinopathy
B-scan ultrasound surveillance while the fundus is obscured to exclude a tear or detachment
Pars plana vitrectomy for non-clearing haemorrhage or when an underlying detachment is suspected
Optimise systemic contributors including glycaemic and blood pressure control and review of anticoagulants
Ophthalmology referral with close monitoring for recurrence
